answer: The SQL in the searchCustomers handler only reads: it selects ID and name from the database table of sales.Customers (sales_Customers), filtered by name LIKE '%<q>%', and writes nothing. Because q is spliced into the string, the effective read set is not bounded by this text: an injected value can read other columns (email, phone) or other tables.

findings.title: searchCustomers reads sales.Customers ID and name, no writes
findings.statement: The native SQL is a single SELECT of columns ID and name from table sales_Customers (entity sales.Customers, db/schema.cds:4) with condition name LIKE '%' || q || '%'; there is no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. It runs on the database directly, not on the OrderService.Customers projection, so projection-level restrictions do not apply to it.

evidence.quote: return cds.run(`SELECT ID, name FROM sales_Customers WHERE name LIKE '%${req.data.q}%'`)
function searchCustomers(q : String) returns array of { ID : UUID; name : String };

findings.test: GET /orders/searchCustomers(q='Acme') as alice returns the Acme row with only ID and name.

findings.title: Interpolated q widens the read set to personal data
findings.statement: The OrderService.Customers projection exposes only ID and name, deliberately hiding email and phone, which are marked as personal data. Since q is interpolated into the SQL text, a crafted value (e.g. a UNION SELECT) can make this statement read email and phone or any other table, so the declared read set (ID, name) is only an upper bound for benign input.

evidence.quote: @readonly entity Customers as projection on sales.Customers { ID, name };

findings.test: GET /orders/searchCustomers(q='x%25'' UNION SELECT email, phone FROM sales_Customers --') as alice; a 200 listing emails shows the wider read.
